Before I give you upload steps, I need to ask a few questions. Uploading a raw DNA file puts a whole genome into a database where other people can match against it. These answers decide whether the upload can go ahead and which settings to choose.

## Questions to answer first

1. **Whose DNA is in the file?** Is it your own test, or someone else's, such as a parent, other relative, client or a minor?
   - If it's someone else's, having their login, managing their kit or being allowed to look at their results is **not** permission to upload it. That person, or a parent or guardian for a minor, needs to agree specifically to GEDmatch and to the visibility and law-enforcement options you'll pick.
   - If the person has died or can't be asked, tell me. Then we decide together whether to go ahead. The default is not to upload.
2. **Which company is the file from**, and is it one test or several? Never combine raw files from different people into one upload. If one person has several tests, upload each as its own kit and decide which one is used for matching.
3. **Who should be able to see and match this kit?** The upload form has you choose a privacy option. Each option controls whether other users can match the kit and whether law-enforcement uploads can match it. I haven't seen the current form, so I can't tell you the exact option names or what each one allows. Read GEDmatch's current Terms of Service and the form's wording yourself. Don't assume that opting out blocks every kind of law-enforcement comparison until the terms say so.
4. **Where do you and the tested person live?** Genetic data is "sensitive" data under the EU and UK GDPR. Some US states also have genetic-privacy laws. Please check which rules apply to you. I can't give you a legal answer.

## The privacy check so far

| Item | Status |
|---|---|
| People | Unknown: whose test is it (question 1)? |
| Data | The raw DNA file (genotypes), plus the kit name or alias and the email address that other users may see |
| Destination | GEDmatch |
| Audience | Depends on the privacy option chosen; unknown until you read the form |
| Controls | Not checked yet: the privacy option, law-enforcement matching and the display name or alias |
| Permission | Unknown: needed from the tested person for GEDmatch and the chosen option |
| Redaction | The genotypes can't be anonymised. You can still choose a display alias and decide which email address other users will see. |
| Retention | Keep the original download and the upload receipt on your own computer, not in a shared folder |
| Jurisdiction | Unknown (question 4) |

Until the unknown items are filled in, the file stays on your computer.

## Plan once permission is clear

1. Open the current upload form. Before submitting, write down the date, each privacy option offered and what the terms say about it.
2. Upload using GEDmatch's current instructions for that company's file. Save the receipt and the kit number.
3. Wait until the kit's status says processing is finished. GEDmatch's help says this typically takes 24–48 hours, but go by the status shown, not the clock.
4. First, check matching against a known relative's kit with a One-to-One comparison and save that result as a baseline. After that, run One-to-Many. One-to-Many and One-to-One are free. Segment Search, triangulation, phasing and Lazarus are paid "Tier 1" tools.

Tell me whose test it is and which options you're considering. If the answers show informed permission, I'll go through the upload steps with you. I haven't uploaded anything or contacted anyone.

I've written a draft, but I changed one thing you asked for. **It doesn't tell her you think she's your half-sister.** When the person you're writing to may be a half-sibling, the first message should state facts only and leave her to work out the relationship herself. She'll likely be able to, because the site shows her the same match. You can't take back a first message, and it may be the only contact you get. A sentence like "I think you're my half-sister" can also tell her something about her own parent that she doesn't know, before she has agreed to hear it.

## Draft (for you to send yourself through the testing site's messages)

> **Subject:** Our DNA match on [site]
>
> Hello [her display name],
>
> My name is [your name]. I'm writing about my own DNA test on [site] (profile/kit: [your kit name]), which shows a match with [her kit or username]. If you manage this test for someone else, I'd be grateful if you could pass this message on to them.
>
> I was born in [place] in [year]. [Optional, only if you're comfortable: I know very little about my [father's / mother's] side of the family.]
>
> Our match is one of the closest on my list, and I'd like to understand how we're connected. Would you be willing to tell me where your parents' families come from?
>
> There's no pressure at all. Reply whenever suits you, or not at all, and I'll respect that.
>
> [Your first name]

**What I left out, and why:**
- **"Half-sister," and the name of the parent you suspect you share.** Either one gives away the conclusion. If you want to name that parent, you decide that after she replies.
- **Shared cM and longest segment.** At this level the number alone points to a relationship. She can see it on her own match list anyway. Copy the figure exactly from the site in a later message if she replies.
- **A tree link.** Only add one if the tree hides living relatives or you've checked who can see them.

Fill in only details you've actually seen on the site, and don't estimate any value.

The recipe I followed bases this approach on Leah Larkin's model letter, ["Letter to a Birth Parent"](https://thednageek.com/letter-to-a-birth-parent/) (The DNA Geek, 2017). I couldn't open it here, so I haven't reproduced it. It's worth reading before you send.

## Before you send: privacy check

You haven't sent me any match details, so some of these are still open:

- **People:** you; the match (living); the parent you may share and that parent's partner or partners (assume they're living). Am I right that you're the tester and you're writing about your own kit?
- **Data:** a possible relationship and possible unexpected parentage. The draft discloses only your name, your birthplace and year, and the fact that you match.
- **Destination and audience:** the site's own messaging, read by her or by whoever manages her kit. Check her profile and any linked tree for signs that someone else, such as a family genealogist, runs the kit. If so, you decide whether to write to that person.
- **Controls:** which site is this? Before you send, note the date and what your own profile and tree show her.
- **Jurisdiction:** where do you and she live? Genetic data counts as sensitive data under the GDPR, for example. Please confirm which rules apply to you.
- **Retention:** first, save dated screenshots of the match entry (kit names, shared cM, longest segment) and of any linked tree. Keep them on your own device only, because matches sometimes go private later.

## Two things to settle first

1. **Is she really a half-sibling?** Half-sibling levels of shared DNA overlap with several other close relationships, such as a grandparent, aunt or uncle, or a double first cousin. Endogamy can also push the numbers up. The match alone doesn't show which one applies. Shared matches, the X-DNA or Y-DNA results of other tested relatives, and records can tell them apart. I can help with that before or after you write.
2. **Who could this affect?** The parent you may share, and their family, could also be affected. Think about that before you send rather than after.

## After you send

- Log the date, recipient, kit, site and what you disclosed.
- If she doesn't reply, record it as **"no response as of [date]"**, not as a refusal. Don't send reminders or a more direct follow-up. Wait at least a year before writing to her again, and send a fresh, careful message rather than a nudge. Meanwhile you could ask a more distant cousin on the same line for tree facts.
- If she replies "I don't recognise those names," record it as **"does not recognise"**, not "no connection."

Tell me the site, the match's display name and what the match page shows, and I'll fill in the draft. Nothing has been sent.

The outreach recipe I'm following says a first message to a possible half-sibling should give only checkable facts and then ask for help. She can work out the connection herself and decide whether and how to reply. A first message is effectively final. If the guess is wrong, or the shared parent's story is unknown or painful in her family, the message can't be taken back and she may never reply.

There's a second reason. Without your numbers I can't treat "half-sister" as established. Other relationships, such as aunt, grandparent or double first cousin, can share a similar amount of DNA, so it's a hypothesis to test.

## Draft (you send it yourself, through the testing site's messaging)

> Hi [her username, or "whoever manages this kit"],
>
> My name is [your first name, or full name if you're comfortable]. I'm writing about my own DNA test, [your kit name], which matches the kit [her kit name / username] on [site].

I can give you the general method now. To name actual record collections, I need some context first: **where and when was he born, what was his religion or denomination, and what do you already have that names him?** Examples are a death certificate, marriage record, census entry, will, family tree or DNA matches. The records that can name a man's parents depend entirely on the place, the period and the church, so I won't guess them.

Here is the method I'd use whatever the answers are.

## 1. Define exactly what you're proving

Your question is "Person X, born about [year] in [place], was the son of A and B." That claim breaks into two parts:
- **Identity:** these records describe your 4th great-grandfather and not another man with the same name.
- **Kinship:** that man was the son of these particular parents.

Records can settle the first part and leave the second open.

## 2. Check the generations below him first

Every generation from you up to his children needs its own documented parent–child link. If one of those links is questionable, stop there and prove it before building on it. Any later DNA argument also depends on that chain being solid.

## 3. Collect every record of his life, not just his birth

Parents are often named in records made late in life. Depending on place and period, these may include:
- a marriage entry or licence (some name the parents)
- a death or burial entry, weighed by who gave the information
- probate records, deeds and land transfers from the parents' estate (heirs, "my son")
- censuses (relationship column, birthplace, others in the household)
- church registers (baptisms of his children, with sponsors who may be relatives)
- tax rolls
- court records
- obituaries

## 4. Build a table with one row per record

Use columns for:
- event date and recording date (as separate columns)
- place and occupation
- age as stated, and how that form defined age
- spouse and children
- associates: witnesses, sponsors, neighbours
- signature or mark
- informant

Sort the table by these columns, not by name. A name alone is the weakest way to tell two people apart.

## 5. Search for other men with the same name

Search the same place and period for every other man with his name, and for every couple with the proposed parents' names. Keep each candidate in a separate file so their records don't mix. If only one candidate turns up, that is still only a candidate: many records are lost or not indexed. Name the detail that would tell him apart from a namesake you haven't found, such as age, wife, place or household, and check it.

## 6. Weigh the evidence, don't count it

- Classify each statement by whether its informant had firsthand knowledge of that particular fact.
- Five online trees copying one claim count as one unverified claim.
- A headstone, death certificate and obituary that agree are often one family member's statement.

## 7. Write down the hypothesis and how it could be disproved

For example: "H1: A and B were his parents." Keep the strongest rival, H2, and also "unknown." Then name a search whose result would differ under H1 and H2, and what result would disprove H1. Some ways that can happen:
- the proposed father's will or estate leaves him out where his siblings appear
- a parent's household list has no son of the right age
- the chronology is impossible, such as a mother past childbearing age or a birth more than about 10 months after the father's death

Many failed searches prove nothing unless the record should exist and survives for that place and year.

## 8. If no record states the parents, correlate the indirect evidence in writing

This is often the case before civil registration. Build the case from things like:
- heirs in the parents' probate
- land he received from them
- shared sponsors and witnesses
- the same neighbours in old and new places
- children's names echoing the proposed parents, as supporting evidence only and never the foundation

The argument has to be written out step by step, not just asserted.

## 9. DNA, if you can use it

At five generations back, autosomal DNA is weak on its own. Look for matches who descend from the proposed parents through his siblings, and document each match's line to the shared ancestors before counting them. The paper descent and the DNA sharing must both support the same hypothesis. A Y-DNA test of a direct male-line descendant can test the surname line, but it can't identify a specific father. If his family came from a community where many people intermarried (for example Ashkenazi Jewish, Acadian or some island populations), DNA results overstate how closely people are related.

## 10. Decide whether it's proved

The conclusion holds only if the records come from a thorough search, every conflict between them is explained, and the written argument can be defended. You make the final decision on that, not a tool or a hint. If it falls short, record the parents as a hypothesis "supported so far" and list the next search that could settle it.

Once you tell me the place and period, his religion and what you hold, I'll turn this into a list of specific collections, ranked by which are most likely to name his parents, plus the test that could disprove the link.

Proving the parents of a 4th great-grandfather usually means building one written argument from several records. A single document that names his parents may not exist, and a tree that says so isn't proof. This is the general method. The specific record collections depend on where and when he lived, so there are some questions at the end.

## 1. Check the links between you and him first

Before you work on his parents, check that each generation from you up to him is sourced: you to parent, parent to grandparent, and so on through six links. If one of those links is weak, his parents may not be your ancestors at all. Fix a shaky link first, or label everything above it as conditional.

## 2. Write down exactly what you're testing

State it as a claim to test, for example: "John Doe, born about 1790 in [place], was the son of William and Mary Doe." Then note where that claim came from. Ten online trees that copy each other count as one unverified claim. If a compiled genealogy says "probably" or "apparently," keep that wording; finding no other record doesn't turn it into a fact.

## 3. Collect every record of his own life

Make a table with one row per record: birth or baptism, marriage, children's baptisms, censuses or tax lists, land, probate, military, church, death and burial. Give each detail its own column: age, place, occupation, spouse, neighbours, witnesses, and whether he signed or made a mark. Record the event date and the date the record was made separately. Then sort the table by each of those columns, not by name. Sorting this way can show two men mixed into one, or one man who looks like two.

## 4. Look for records that state the parentage

Depending on the place and period, these could be:
- a baptism or birth entry naming his parents
- a marriage entry naming his parents (later marriages sometimes ask when earlier ones didn't)
- his father's will, estate file or heirs' deed that names him as a son
- a deed of gift, guardianship or apprenticeship record
- his death record, though the informant probably knew his parents' names only secondhand

Judge each statement by whether the person who gave it would have known that fact firsthand. Don't judge a whole record as reliable or unreliable.

## 5. If nothing states it, build an indirect argument and write it out

Research the proposed parents' family as fully as his:
- Does he fit their household lists by age?
- Did he move with them?
- Was he a witness, surety or neighbour on their deeds?
- Was he a sponsor at their children's baptisms, or they at his?
- Did he share in their estates, and how?

Write the chain of reasoning down. Indirect evidence proves nothing until the argument is written.

## 6. Search for rivals on purpose

- Search the same place and period for **other men with his name**, and for **other couples with the proposed parents' names**. Keep each candidate in a separate file so their records don't get mixed together.
- Rule out a candidate only on positive evidence, such as a burial in childhood or a documented family elsewhere. "No later record found" doesn't rule anyone out.
- If one candidate is left standing, he is still only a candidate. Name the detail that would tell him apart from a namesake you haven't found yet.

## 7. Name what would disprove the link, and look for it

Examples:
- The father's will or estate leaves him out when the other children are named. Check first whether he had already received land or money.
- The father died more than about 10 months before he was born.
- The mother was outside childbearing age.
- The father's household had no boy of the right age.
- A same-named baptism points to a different couple.

Do these impossibility checks before you accept any merge.

## 8. DNA can support the argument but won't settle it alone

His parents are your 5th great-grandparents, so any DNA matches through them will be distant. A match counts only after that tester's descent to the couple is documented generation by generation. The most useful testers descend from the proposed parents' other children. Judge the quality of each match rather than counting matches. Endogamy, meaning a community that often married within itself, makes matches look closer than they are. The DNA and the documents should end up in one argument, not two separate verdicts. Before asking a relative to test or sharing anyone's match data, get their consent and check the destination's privacy settings.

## 9. Write the conclusion

Write it as a proof summary or proof argument. It should cite each source, explain each conflict rather than going with the majority, and include a dated log of searches that found nothing. Deciding whether the standard is met is your call, not the software's.

**To name actual record collections, I need:**
1. Where and roughly when he was born, married and died, and his religion or denomination.
2. Who the proposed parents are, and where that claim comes from (a tree, a book, family story or a record).
3. Which records you already have for him and for the proposed parents.
4. Whether you or relatives have DNA tests, and on which sites.

With those, I can suggest the specific registers, probate courts or archives to search first.

## Why I won't state a probability

The chance that 212 cM means second cousin depends on a model built from simulated or observed data. A language model that produces such a number is making it up. A shared amount doesn't map to one relationship either. It fits a range of candidates whose sharing overlaps.

At 212 cM, second cousin is plausible, but so are several other relationships. These include:
- second cousin (2C)
- first cousin twice removed (1C2R)
- half first cousin once removed
- half first cousin
- first cousin once removed (1C1R)
- half great-aunt
- other more-distant "half" and "removed" relationships

Half and full relationships often can't be told apart from total cM alone.

## How to get a real figure

1. **Use DNA Painter's Shared cM tool** (dnapainter.com/tools/sharedcmv4). Enter only the number 212. No names are needed, so no one's identity leaves your device.
2. **Read the probability table carefully.** The tool gives one probability to a whole group of relationships. That group includes second cousin alongside 1C2R, half 1C1R and others. Don't report the group's percentage as the chance of second cousin alone.
3. **Note where the probabilities come from.** The tool credits its probabilities to The DNA Geek's statistics, which trace to AncestryDNA's white paper. They fit Ancestry's totals most directly. If your 212 cM comes from another company, say so whenever you quote the figure.
4. **Open the histograms for second cousin and the competing relationships.** Note where 212 falls in each. The percentages shown there describe that relationship's spread of reported values. They are not the chance that it's the right relationship.

| Field | Value | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|

# Planning the interview with your aunt

The point is to capture her account well enough that you can tell, years from now, what she said, what someone else suggested to her, and what you added later. Treat what she tells you as her account to check against records, not as facts to add straight to the tree.

## 1. Before the visit

- **Recording law.** Look up the rules where each of you will be. Some U.S. states require everyone's consent, including for conversations in person. If you record over the phone across state lines, the stricter state's rule can apply. In the UK and EU, a recording of a living person is personal data. Keeping it in the family is usually exempt, but sharing or publishing it may not be. Record openly either way.
- **Her capacity to agree.** If you think memory problems might stop her understanding what the recording is for, explain things in plain words. You could also have a carer or relative she trusts sit in, with their role agreed beforehand. That person's agreement doesn't replace hers. If she can't give informed agreement, keep any recording for private family memory only, and never deposit or publish it.
- **Prompts to bring.** Pick a few specific things: a photograph, an object, a family recipe, or an event she lived through. If she grew up in a census year you can access, bring her household's census page too.
- **Equipment.**
  - Clip a lapel microphone on her.
  - Make sure your questions are recorded as well, with a second mic or by putting the recorder between you.
  - Do a short test recording of both voices and play it back.
  - If you can, run a phone as a backup recorder.

## 2. Getting consent at the start

With the recorder running, say something like:

> "Today is [date]. I'm [name] talking with [aunt's name] at [place]. Others present: [names]. We're talking about the family when you were growing up. The recording is for [the family / me / a family archive], and it will be used for [family history]. You can skip any question, take a break, or stop at any time. Is it all right with you to record this?"

Signed written consent is better, but her spoken consent on the recording is acceptable.

## 3. During the interview

- **Keep the recorder running the whole time.** Don't stop and restart it, and glance at the level meter now and then.
- **Use open, bounded questions.** Ask "What do you remember about the house on…?" rather than "Your grandfather was born in Kyiv, wasn't he?" Never suggest the answer you're hoping for.
- **With photographs, start with the setting.** Ask about the place, the buildings, the vehicles and the season before asking who the people are. If she names someone, write it down as her identification and note why she thinks so. Don't judge identity by resemblance yourself.
- **After an important question, wait quietly.** Give her time to remember.
- **Ask about the oldest person she remembers from childhood.** This often brings out older stories. When she passes on something she heard, follow up with:
  - Who told you that?
  - When was it, and how old were you?
  - How would that person have known?
- **Census page prompt.** Show her own household's entry, read out the neighbours listed before and after it, and ask what she recalls about them. Being listed next to someone doesn't prove kinship or that they lived together.
- **Watch for cues from others.** If a relative in the room prompts her ("Do you remember when…"), note who said it and roughly when. Anything only the prompter brought up stays the prompter's account.
- **Watch for strain.** If she struggles or seems to be trying too hard to help, don't press. Stop, note that you stopped, and check those details against documents later. Anything that only came out after repeated pressing should be marked "possibly reconstructed."
- **Respect a "no."** If she doesn't want to talk about a topic, move on.

## 4. At the end and right after

- **Confirm the terms of use.** Ideally she signs a simple release or joint statement of intent. Otherwise, record her saying what's allowed. Note any limits, such as "family only" or "not until after I'm gone."
- **Explain what sharing means.** Once a recording is posted publicly or given to an archive, it may be impossible to take back fully. If you can, offer to let her review it before it goes beyond the family.
- **Check the file the same day.** Make sure it's complete and audible, then copy it to a second place on your own storage. If a passage didn't record or can't be heard, write that down. Never fill it in from memory or from what you asked.

## 5. What to keep

- **The original recording, unedited.** Make edited extracts as separate files.
- **A session register.** Note the date, place, everyone present, how consent and release were given, the prompts used (for example "photo #3"), the file names, and any point where you stopped.
- **A statement log.** For each claim, note:
  - who said it
  - who prompted it
  - the time in the recording
  - whether it's her words, your transcript, a paraphrase or your interpretation
  - any uncertain names, marked as uncertain rather than tidied into a definite spelling
- **For stories she was told:** the chain of tellers, from whom to whom, with the occasion and how each teller could know.

If other relatives remember the same events differently, record each version as that person's own account. Don't merge them into one.

# Proving your 4th great-grandfather's parents: a plan

Which records to search depends on where and when he lived, and I don't know that yet. The method below works anywhere. I'll need a few details from you, listed at the end, before I can name actual record collections.

## 1. Define what you're proving
Write the claim as a sentence you can test: "Person X, born about [year] in [place], was the son of A and B." Use what records say about him, not what online trees say. You're proving a parent–child link, not just collecting records with the right surname. Five trees that copy one claim count as one unchecked claim.

## 2. Pin down who he is before looking for his parents
Collect every record of him: baptism or birth, marriage, censuses, tax lists, land, probate, church, military and death. Put one record per row in a table, with columns for:
- dates and places, keeping event date and recording date separate
- wife, children, occupation
- neighbours, witnesses and sponsors
- whether he signed his name or made a mark

Sort the table by each of these details, not by name. A name alone is the weakest way to tell people apart. Run some basic checks too: no births in impossible years, no being in two places at once.

## 3. Look for other men with his name
Search the same place and period for other men with his name, and for other couples with the proposed parents' names. Keep each one in his own file so their records don't get mixed together. Compare them on details other than the name, such as wife, age, land and neighbours. Finding only one candidate doesn't prove it's him, because many records are lost or not indexed.

## 4. Look for records that name his parents directly
Depending on the place and period, these might include:
- a baptism or birth record naming the parents
- a marriage record naming the parents
- a parent's will, estate file or heirs' deed naming him as a son
- a death record naming his parents

Judge each statement by whether the person who gave it would have known firsthand. On a death record, the informant usually knew the death firsthand but the parents' names only secondhand.

## 5. If nothing names them, build a written argument from indirect clues
Link the clues together explicitly, in writing:
- **Land:** land passing from the candidate father to him, or deeds dividing an estate among heirs
- **People around the family:** relatives and neighbours who keep turning up as witnesses, bondsmen or godparents, and families who moved together
- **The candidate father's household:** does a son of the right age appear, and disappear when your man sets up his own household?
- **Naming patterns:** these can point to a search, but they are supporting evidence, never the foundation

Cautions:
- A will or heir list isn't a full list of children. A son may be left out because he already received his share.
- "No record found" isn't evidence until you've ruled out lost records, gaps in coverage and indexing errors. Log every search with its date.

- Write H1 (the preferred parents), H2 (a rival family or namesake) and H3 (parents unknown).
- Record which later conclusions depend on H1. For example, the candidate's parents become your 5th great-grandparents only if H1 holds.

- **Watch for shared ancestry.** In communities where families intermarried, matches can share DNA through other lines and look closer than they are.
- **Judge quality, not count.** A few well-documented matches outweigh many undocumented ones. Even when DNA and paper agree, that's evidence, not proof by itself.

## 8. Write the proof argument, and judge it yourself
Write up:
- your sources and how much weight each statement carries
- how you resolved each conflict
- what your searches didn't find, and why that absence matters
- how the clues fit together

I can draft it and point out weak spots. You decide whether it meets the standard.

1. Where and roughly when did he live, and what was his religion?
2. What records do you already have for him?
3. Do you have candidate parents in mind, and where does that idea come from: a record, a tree or family tradition?

# Is this an 1880s photo of your great-grandmother?

## 1. Is it from the 1880s?

| Clue | Source | What it dates | Direction | What it gives you |

| "Card-mounted studio portrait" | Description only | The format | A soft range only | Can't be used until the card type is named (carte de visite or cabinet card) and dated from a cited reference |
| Pencil note "Mother" | Writer and date unknown | Only when the note was written | None | Says nothing about the date |

- **If it might be a reproduction**, the studio dates the mount, not the moment the photo was taken.
- **Clothing and hairstyle** can only show the earliest possible date. For a woman in her 30s or 40s they can't set a latest date, because older people often kept earlier styles.
- **No single summary should close the window.** Different sources often give a studio different working years, so write down each source's range separately.

3. **Big Y-700 for both men gives the best answer.** If you share a branch on FamilyTreeDNA's Time Tree, that branch's estimated date for your common ancestor is the figure to use. It comes with a confidence interval and can shift as more men test.

### The Smith surname cuts both ways

- **A shared surname with a close match is a good lead**, better than the same GD with an unrelated surname.
- **It doesn't make the connection recent.** Smith is a job name, and it was probably taken up independently by many unrelated families. So the surname helps less here than a rare one would. Check when hereditary surnames came into use in the region your line comes from. Your link may predate them.
- **Treat it as a hypothesis to test against records.** Compare your earliest known paternal ancestors and their places. If you're also an autosomal match (FamilyTreeDNA's Family Finder), that points to a fairly recent connection worth working on. If you aren't, a distant link is still possible.

### Keep a note of

- the test level each of you took and the level compared
- the GD reported
- the marker values, if you can see them
- the TiP output and the date you ran it

### Before anything leaves your account

Joining a surname project, or entering marker values into an outside tool, shares a living person's genetic data. Messaging the match means contacting a living person. Clear the privacy checks for each of these first. Nothing here needs you to do any of them yet.

If you tell me your earliest known paternal ancestor, the match's, and the levels you each tested, I can help plan which records would confirm or rule out the connection.

# GD 2 at Y-37 with another Smith: how many generations?

**There isn't a reliable generation count to give you.** A genetic distance (GD) of 2 at 37 markers says the two of you probably share a paternal line. It doesn't say when your common ancestor lived. That ancestor could have lived within a few generations or several centuries ago. Any single figure, such as "about 5 generations," would be made up.

## Why GD 2 can't be turned into generations

- **Mutations happen at random times.** Two lines can pick up two differences in one generation or stay identical for many. GD measures how different you are, not how much time has passed.
- **GD isn't the number of markers that differ.** FamilyTreeDNA scores most markers step by step, so a single marker that differs by two steps can produce GD 2 alone. Back mutations and parallel mutations can also hide what actually happened.
- **37 markers is a low resolution.** Estimated ranges get wider as the number of markers drops. Men who look close at 37 markers often turn out to be more distant at 111 markers or on Big Y. Some matches disappear entirely once tested at higher levels.
- **Even FamilyTreeDNA's own STR estimates ran too recent.** In 2023 they replaced their older STR-based timing because it often put the common ancestor too close in time. Their ranges are now built from Big Y branch ages.

## What to look at instead

1. **Open the TiP (time predictor) report for this match on FamilyTreeDNA.** Write down the range and the confidence level it gives. In one published case the report gave "born 1500–1850" and the documented ancestor was born in 1798, inside that range. Treat the middle of a range as the middle of a wide band, not as the answer.
2. **Check which markers differ, if you can see both sets of values.** Find out whether the GD comes from one marker differing by two steps or from two separate markers. Use only markers you both tested, and leave any missing or unclear value unresolved rather than counting it as a match.
3. **Upgrade the right tests.** Big Y-700 on both of you gives the most useful answer. It includes the 111-marker test, and FamilyTreeDNA's Time Tree would then date your shared branch with a confidence range. Upgrading to Y-111 narrows things somewhat, but only if he upgrades too. In a 2025 example, men of one surname matched within GD 2 at Y-37. Big Y-700, followed by a record, tied them to one common ancestor. The close Y-37 result justified the upgrade but didn't show how the men were related.
4. **Let records do the placing.** Compare both of your earliest known paternal ancestors and where they lived. Smith is such a common name that matching surnames could mean the families were named separately and connect from before surnames were inherited. The DNA has to be checked against a documented paper trail.

**One caution about contacting him:** asking him for his marker values, his tree or an upgrade means approaching a living person about his genetic data. Before you do, think about what you'd share and what you'd ask him to share. If you'd like help drafting the message, I can take you through that step by step.

It tells them to record the range and confidence level, and warns against treating the middle of a range as the answer.

The answer doesn't conclude non-paternity from the genetic distance (GD) or from the surname. Its surname caveat only says Smith families may have been named separately and connect from before surnames were inherited, which isn't a non-paternity verdict. It leaves placing the relationship to records.
